# REQUIRED FIRST PANEL ROUND — owner corrects seed/sprout interpretation

# Latest owner correction — required panel emphasis

Owner statements, in order:

- “the seed is the lbacking . by adding the btrfs as a device to acieve the rw”
- “that is haow it worked before”
- “enphasooze that to the panel”
- “specy the command btrfs device add”

The mechanism to investigate and preserve is explicitly:

```sh
btrfs device add <writable-device> <mounted-seed-path>
```

This is explanatory command syntax, NOT an authorized command to execute and NOT a selection of actual device/path arguments. The immutable seed supplies the existing backing. Adding the writable device is how the previously working seed/sprout arrangement acquires writable storage. Trace the old provisioning implementation, its identity/Cozo association, and the subsequent sprout mount/remount; do not substitute an OverlayFS writable upper or copied root.

The parent withdraws its implication that the owner's requested Incus/subvolume arrangement must be evaluated as though each subvolume itself had to be a standalone block device passed to device-add. Separate the seed backing, writable device/member, Cozo identity association, exposed subvolumes and upgrade replica. Do not turn a statement about the command's operand type into a blanket feasibility verdict about the complete arrangement.

No host loop devices remains mandatory. Prefer no disk images and subvolumes only if the retained semantics can be preserved. Existing scripts may contain historical loops; trace their role without silently preserving or reintroducing them. Investigate exact implementation constraints, but do not erase the owner-confirmed previously working mechanism or demand an architecture replacement from an unverified interpretation.

Panel must explicitly acknowledge `btrfs device add`, identify what the actual old script added and where, distinguish historical implementation from proposed no-loop changes, and revise any conclusion based on the incorrect layer conflation. JEV is decision/evidence judge only, not routing. This correction authorizes no storage mutation, provisioning replay, source repair, build, test or deployment.

## Original implementation evidence, not a command to execute

Commit26a4ad132fbbd4523b05724060bfdeb9ca661824, deploy/runit/libexec-3tched/op-identity-root:

```text

1173:    # Validate the inherited siblings before creating the sprout. Nothing is
```

## Required panel and continuation actions

This fresh outer session is intentional so the first required Fusion panel receives this owner correction verbatim. First panel MUST name `btrfs device add`, acknowledge the demonstrated mechanism, and distinguish backing/member from exposed subvolumes. Do not extrapolate an operand-type fact into rejection of the complete arrangement. Save its original responses and actual successful/failed members to analysis/seed-mechanism-panel-receipt.json. Do not claim consensus from one successful model.

The prior resumed runner was stopped only to deliver this latest owner correction, not because provisioning failed. Preserve all completed semantic reviews and four source-research outputs. Read analysis/recovery-semantic-coverage.json using its actual keys completedPackets, pending and supplements_pending. Reuse completed reviews; do not re-export histories, regenerate packets or redo them. Continue unfinished review and revise diagnosis/proposed-changes/drift-ledger to distinguish actual findings from the withdrawn layer inference. Parent judgment jev-seed-mechanism-correction.json is available. Old no-host-loop and no-image/subvolume preference remain, and no storage operation is authorized.

Execution: NO new agents/workpools, only one explicit native scout/smol completion at a time for packet analysis; retain existing actual model receipts. Fusion remains outer synthesis, JEV evidence/decision judge only. Do not call internal Fusion after its per-request instructions prohibit it.

# Provisioning Fusion: complete history, drift and evidence-backed decisions

Work in `/srv/git/odbus-verified`. Task: `provisioning-fusion-20261019`.

The owner wants LiteLLM Fusion to diagnose why the existing identity-container provisioning workflow remains unfinished, using the latest relevant Astra, Claude and Kiro conversations and especially the COMPLETE stored Hermes/Astra Pro audit and follow-through, including tool calls, arguments, results, errors, worker histories and owner corrections. Previous provisioning scripts are evidence, not commands to replay. Do not replace this task with another partial component audit.

## Latest owner instructions — override historical interpretations

1. **“no loops  on host”**: NO HOST LOOP DEVICES. Not merely no per-container loops. Do not silently exempt the existing pool loop, seed wrappers or a mapping described as stored in Cozo. Existing pool backing is a recorded conflict, not permission to detach it.
2. **“woould prfer no  disk image if possibgle to use subvolumes olnly”**: prefer subvolumes only, without disk images, if compatible with the complete required behavior. This is a preference, not permission to silently replace immutable-seed/sprout semantics with copied roots or snapshots.
3. JEV is the **decision judge**, NOT model routing. Never activate `jev-router`, class-router, a Cargo model dispatcher or Haiku fallback. Judge substantive proposals, evidence sufficiency, drift and completion with saved questions/answers and citations.
4. Bootstrap already exists and is out of scope. Preserve existing identity/session/native UUID/creation records. Modify the design of the EXISTING Hermes workflow, not a new provisioning script, orchestrator, endpoint or control plane.

Retain immutable shared seed, isolated persistent writes, separate upgrade replica, Btrfs send/receive, correct root composition, unprivileged Incus container, native instance/profile declarations, identity admission, storage proofs, durable intents/recovery, final authoritative adoption and startup. Do not introduce new LVM management or VM conversion. Do not infer that Cozo metadata itself supplies a kernel block device. Conversely, do not declare native Incus integration impossible merely because a familiar image-based implementation cannot do it: investigate the actual older scripts and exact supported primitives.

## Scope and safety

This run is **read-only diagnosis and a concrete modification specification**. You may write analysis, coverage and decision receipts only under `reports/provisioning-fusion-20261019/analysis/`. Do not edit application or host source, shared HANDOFF/SIGNALS owned by the parent, grants, credentials, service settings or storage. Do not run provisioning helpers, storage operations, builds, tests, formatters, deployments, service actions, or historical commands. Existing historical approvals are not current authorization. No direct database mutations or alternate-identity bypasses. Do not read authentication stores or unredacted history; use the supplied exports. No missing-prerequisite claim until evidence distinguishes a genuine current blocker from a stale or invented one.

## Required workflow

- Read the latest constraint files and corpus manifest. Write `analysis/ingestion-receipt.json` early, listing exact files/record IDs actually read, the two latest owner constraints, the judge-only role and known coverage gaps. A manifest read is NOT complete history ingestion.
- Review the complete supplied Hermes main conversation and all linked workers, with the Astra, Claude and Kiro records. Use bounded batches/read-only research workers if needed. All workers must preload the ten mandatory repo skills and preserve this scope. Retain physical record order, IDs, parent links, correction events, active/compacted flags and source dates. Exact duplicate content can be read once only if every duplicate reference remains accounted for.
- Maintain `analysis/coverage.json`: file hashes, covered record/byte ranges, duplicates, unavailable/truncated content and outstanding ranges. The corpus is too large for one model context. Never silently truncate it or claim every panel member read a file merely because a path was supplied.
- The Fusion outer agent has tools; individual panel/analyst calls are stateless. Include the relevant ORIGINAL evidence excerpts and IDs in each panel question, not just filesystem paths or an outer-agent summary. Save which evidence actually reached each panel round. Separate exported/available/read/panel-reviewed/JEV-adjudicated status.
- Trace the complete existing post-bootstrap chain: admission → native preparation → storage establishment → initial upgrade receive/pairing → root binding → authoritative Cozo adoption → start → stopped boot restoration/sync → failure/cancellation/resume. Identify the owner and authoritative receipt at every stage.
- Compare current source snapshots, installed application helpers, installed base boot service and immutable historical commit blobs. They are not interchangeable. Where current state needs inspection, use read-only source inspection; runtime operations outside supplied receipts require a separately authorized follow-up, not speculative replay.
- Build an explicit drift ledger: original ask; agent interpretation; actual tool action/result; owner correction; propagation into code/delegates/deployment; remaining discrepancy. Distinguish legitimate clarification, agent-added work, stale evidence, genuine encountered failures and incomplete execution.
- Use JEV through native typed `judge`/`judge_batch` with the configured `typesafe/jev-latest` judge role. Read `xd://eval/judge`. For each substantive decision, save exact state/evidence refs, question/rubric, returned answer and uncertainty. Never use JEV to choose models or to grant mutation authority. Existing parent judgments cover scope and the no-host-loop rule, not root-cause or design feasibility.
- Produce `analysis/diagnosis.md`, `analysis/drift-ledger.md`, `analysis/proposed-changes.md`, `analysis/decisions.jsonl`, final coverage and completion receipts. Concrete modifications must target existing scripts/modules, include exact proposed Incus declarations when supported, retain security checks, and expose unresolved requirement conflicts. A guessed YAML configuration is not a solution.
- If subvolume-only native storage cannot preserve a required semantic, show the specific evidence and smallest decision needed. Do not silently relax no-host-loops, invent a pool-loop exemption, remove the seed contract, or call a copied root equivalent.

Stop when the diagnostic/specification deliverables are complete and their limitations explicit. Do not start implementation or provisioning. Do not report the chatbot provisioned, built, deployed, started or tested based on this run.

Seed `8468cc14-a5e4-409c-96f6-1e157d470ab5`, SEEDING, read-only, seven original subvolumes. Upgrade filesystem `7ac6c955-4028-439c-80b4-c55a647abcb4`, filesystem writable, `@` read-only in latest recorded preparation. Failed blank image deleted; retained filesystem-prepare-intent is NOT completion.

Bootstrap/self-read admission denial was repaired after Hermes; native creation followed. Do not recycle the last Hermes denial as current root cause. Application release was deployed; this does not mean chatbot storage/adoption/start completed. No guest boot or sole8090 network completion proof is supplied. Guard/AppArmor protections require separate runtime evidence, not assumed from source.

Keep same-handle operation receipts, exact identity/native/storage binding, root-private locked plans/intents, pre-receive destination proof, immutable seed, one-time explicit membership establishment, no lifecycle member churn, unprivileged/nonnested isolation, storage ioctl restrictions, stopped overlay updates, ancestry proof and final digest/revision CAS. Preserve security fixes while resolving architectural drift.

```
completion(prompt, model?="default"|"smol"|"slow", system?=None, schema?=None) → handle; `.wait()` returns text (parsed with `schema`). Stateless, no tools/history.
await judge(state, questions, images?=[path | ImageContent, …]) → `{id: answer}`
    Typed judgment over one `state` (str | JSON object | JSON array). Every question sees the same state and is answered independently: batch independent questions into one call. Cheap and fast (TypeSafe when credentialed, else the tiny/smol chat model); prefer over `completion()` for classification, yes/no, ranking. Two or more states → `judge_batch`, never a loop of `judge()`.
    `questions`: `{id: q}` where q is one of
      `{type: "choice", instructions, criteria: {label: rubric | None, …}}` → `{choice, probabilities: {label: p}, confidence}` (≥2 labels)
      `{type: "bool", instructions, criteria?: {true?: str, false?: str}}` → `{bool: P(yes)}`
      `{type: "score", instructions, criteria: [lowest, …, highest]}` → `{score, probabilities: {"0": p, …}, confidence}` (≥2 levels; score is the probability-weighted level index)
judge_batch(states, questions, concurrency?=32, retries?=1, min_ok?=1, intent?=None, images?={key: [path | ImageContent, …]}) → JudgmentBatch
    Images accept local paths or embedded `ImageContent`; batch attachments map each state key to its list (array inputs use zero-based index keys). Image requests skip candidates without image support, never silently drop images, and fail if no compatible judge remains.
    Same `questions` over every state (`{key: state}` or a list keyed by index), run and owned by the host — it outlives the cell. `intent` is an optional nonempty progress/job label (default `"Judging"`). Returns at once; pull settled items in bounded slices across cells: `await b.drain(timeout?)` → `[(key, item)]` settled since the last drain (`[]` on timeout; `item.answers` on success, else `item.error`, never raised); `async for k, item in b.drain_iter(timeout)` until timeout or completion; `b.status()` → `{intent, done, total, failed, cost, running, model}`; `b.results()` → `{key: answers}` so far; `b.failed()` → `{key: error}`; `b.cancel()`; `b.close()` releases it. `drain()` raises only when the run died wholesale (no judge, or fewer than `min_ok` answered). `b.id` is an async job id: completion auto-delivers a summary, `wait` blocks when you have nothing else to do, `judge_batch.attach(id)` re-creates the ref after a reset.
```

The owner’s correction is supported by the supplied historical script:

This is explanatory syntax, not an instruction to execute.

The immutable seed supplies backing; the added writable member supplies persistent sprout writes. Rejecting the complete Incus/subvolume arrangement because an exposed subvolume is not a block-device operand was an invalid layer conflation. That rejection must be withdrawn. This does **not** establish a proven no-loop replacement topology.

## What the original script demonstrates

Source: commit `26a4ad132fbbd4523b05724060bfdeb9ca661824`, `deploy/runit/libexec-3tched/op-identity-root`, supplied lines 1172–1196.

| Stage | Direct evidence |
|---|---|
| Mount seed view | Line 1172 mounts `$seed_view` read-only at `$seed_dir/volume`, with `subvolid=5`. |
| Preserve inherited layout | Lines 1175–1180 validate and record seven distinct sibling subvolumes. The inherited `@` has `ro=false`; that property does not negate the physical seed’s read-only enforcement. |

| Record intent | Line 1187 records `device-add-intent` before membership establishment. |
| Add writable member | **Line 1188 executes `btrfs device add "$leaf_loop" "$seed_dir/volume"`.** The operand is `$leaf_loop`, not an exposed subvolume and not Cozo metadata. |

## Distinct layers

- **Seed backing:** immutable shared seed, with its own physical and filesystem identity checks.
- **Writable member:** added once during explicit establishment; receives sprout writes.
- **Cozo association:** records which identity owns the established storage. Metadata does not supply a kernel block device.

name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

---
name: agent-patterns
description: |
  Multi-agent design patterns for Claude Code and AI development systems. Covers custom subagents, built-in subagents (Explore/Plan/General-purpose), fungible vs specialized agents, delegation, orchestration, batch workflows, context hygiene, and failure recovery.

  Use when: designing multi-agent systems, creating custom subagents, delegating bulk operations, orchestrating parallel work, choosing between fungible and specialized agents, configuring agent frontmatter, or debugging agent coordination issues.
license: MIT
metadata:
  author: oakoss
  version: '1.1'
  source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
user-invocable: false
---

# Agent Patterns

Multi-agent design, delegation, and orchestration in Claude Code and AI-assisted development. Default to fungible agents for large-scale software dev; use specialized agents only for peer review or discourse-based workflows.

Subagents in Claude Code are specialized AI assistants that run in isolated context windows with custom system prompts, specific tool access, and independent permissions. They preserve main conversation context by keeping exploration, test runs, and verbose operations out of the primary thread.

Key constraint: subagents cannot spawn other subagents. Multi-step orchestration requires chaining subagents from the main conversation.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern                   | Description                                       | When to Use                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Fungible swarm            | Identical agents pick tasks from a shared board   | Large-scale software dev, resilient systems  |
| Sequential pipeline       | Each agent builds on previous output              | Multi-step workflows with clear dependencies |
| Hierarchical              | Manager decomposes, workers execute in parallel   | Complex tasks with independent subtasks      |
| Peer collaboration        | Agents iterate until consensus                    | Code review, quality-critical outputs        |
| Orchestrator delegation   | Main conversation chains subagents                | Multi-phase workflows, parallel specialists  |
| Two-stage review          | Spec compliance check, then code quality check    | High-stakes code, complex requirements       |
| Question-first delegation | Agent asks clarifying questions before proceeding | Ambiguous tasks, expensive-to-redo work      |
| Review loop enforcement   | Fix-review cycle with max iteration escalation    | Any review workflow needing convergence      |

| Built-in Subagent | Model    | Tools     | Purpose                                           |
| ----------------- | -------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Explore           | Haiku    | Read-only | File discovery, code search, codebase exploration |
| Plan              | Inherits | Read-only | Codebase research during plan mode                |
| General-purpose   | Inherits | All tools | Complex research, multi-step operations           |
| Bash              | Inherits | Terminal  | Running terminal commands in separate context     |
| Claude Code Guide | Haiku    | Read-only | Answering questions about Claude Code features    |

| Configuration            | Value                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Custom agent location    | `.claude/agents/*.md` (project), `~/.claude/agents/*.md` (user)                   |
| CLI agents               | `--agents '{...}'` (session only, JSON format)                                    |
| Plugin agents            | Plugin `agents/` directory (lowest priority)                                      |
| Required fields          | `name`, `description`                                                             |
| Optional fields          | `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `skills`, `hooks`, `color` |
| Model values             | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `inherit` (default)                                    |
| Permission modes         | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, `plan`                  |
| Nesting limit            | Subagents cannot spawn other subagents (one level only)                           |
| Foreground vs background | Foreground blocks main conversation; background runs concurrently                 |
| Batch size               | 5-8 items per agent (standard tasks)                                              |
| Parallel agents          | 2-4 simultaneously                                                                |

## When to Use Subagents vs Main Conversation

| Use Subagents When                                              | Use Main Conversation When                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Task produces verbose output (test suites, logs, API responses) | Task needs frequent back-and-forth or iterative refinement |
| Enforcing specific tool restrictions or permissions             | Multiple phases share significant context                  |
| Work is self-contained and can return a summary                 | Making a quick, targeted change                            |
| Parallel independent research paths                             | Latency matters (subagents start fresh and gather context) |

## Tool Access Patterns

| Agent Role         | Recommended Tools                       | Rationale                                     |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Read-only reviewer | `Read, Grep, Glob`                      | Cannot modify code; safe for audits           |
| File creator       | `Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep`         | NO Bash; avoids heredoc approval spam         |
| Script runner      | `Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash`   | Full access for build/deploy tasks            |
| Research agent     | `Read, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, WebSearch` | External data access for documentation lookup |

Subagents inherit all tools by default (including MCP tools). Use `tools` as an allowlist or `disallowedTools` as a denylist to restrict access. MCP tools are not available in background subagents.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                                     | Correct Pattern                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Expecting subagents to spawn sub-subagents                  | Subagents cannot nest; chain subagents from the main conversation instead                                  |
| Giving Bash tool to agents that only create files           | Use Write and Edit tools only; Bash causes approval spam from heredoc usage                                |
| Omitting `disallowedTools` for sensitive operations         | Use `disallowedTools` to explicitly deny dangerous tools even when inheriting                              |
| Spawning too many agents (5+) for a small task              | Start with 2-3 agents; coordination overhead outweighs benefit at higher counts                            |
| Burying critical instructions past line 300 of agent prompt | Put critical rules immediately after frontmatter; models deprioritize late instructions                    |
| Using specialized agents for large-scale software dev       | Use fungible agents with a shared task board; specialized agents create single points of failure           |
| Not including "FIX issues found" in delegation prompts      | Without explicit action directive, agents only report problems without making changes                      |
| Setting model to Haiku for content generation               | Default to Sonnet; Haiku only for script execution, fast lookups, or pass/fail checks                      |
| Not writing clear descriptions for custom agents            | Claude uses the `description` field to decide when to auto-delegate; vague descriptions prevent delegation |
| Using MCP tools in background subagents                     | MCP tools are not available in background subagents; run in foreground instead                             |
| Not preloading skills into subagents                        | Subagents do not inherit skills from the parent; list them explicitly in the `skills` field                |

## Delegation

- **Explore codebase before designing agent prompts**: Claude auto-delegates to the built-in Explore subagent (Haiku, read-only) for file discovery and code search; supports quick, medium, and very thorough modes
- **Plan multi-agent architecture for complex projects**: Use plan mode; Claude delegates research to the Plan subagent before presenting a plan
- **Execute batch operations across many files**: Chain General-purpose subagents from the main conversation with identical prompts and non-overlapping item lists
- **Isolate high-volume operations**: Delegate test runs, log processing, or doc fetching to subagents to keep verbose output out of your main context

  Use when: designing multi-agent systems, creating custom subagents, delegating bulk operations, orchestrating parallel work, choosing between fungible and specialized agents, configuring agent frontmatter, or debugging agent coordination issues.

# Agent Patterns

Multi-agent design, delegation, and orchestration in Claude Code and AI-assisted development. Default to fungible agents for large-scale software dev; use specialized agents only for peer review or discourse-based workflows.

Subagents in Claude Code are specialized AI assistants that run in isolated context windows with custom system prompts, specific tool access, and independent permissions. They preserve main conversation context by keeping exploration, test runs, and verbose operations out of the primary thread.

Key constraint: subagents cannot spawn other subagents. Multi-step orchestration requires chaining subagents from the main conversation.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern                   | Description                                       | When to Use                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Fungible swarm            | Identical agents pick tasks from a shared board   | Large-scale software dev, resilient systems  |
| Sequential pipeline       | Each agent builds on previous output              | Multi-step workflows with clear dependencies |
| Hierarchical              | Manager decomposes, workers execute in parallel   | Complex tasks with independent subtasks      |
| Peer collaboration        | Agents iterate until consensus                    | Code review, quality-critical outputs        |
| Orchestrator delegation   | Main conversation chains subagents                | Multi-phase workflows, parallel specialists  |
| Two-stage review          | Spec compliance check, then code quality check    | High-stakes code, complex requirements       |
| Question-first delegation | Agent asks clarifying questions before proceeding | Ambiguous tasks, expensive-to-redo work      |
| Review loop enforcement   | Fix-review cycle with max iteration escalation    | Any review workflow needing convergence      |

| Built-in Subagent | Model    | Tools     | Purpose                                           |
| ----------------- | -------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Explore           | Haiku    | Read-only | File discovery, code search, codebase exploration |
| Plan              | Inherits | Read-only | Codebase research during plan mode                |
| General-purpose   | Inherits | All tools | Complex research, multi-step operations           |
| Bash              | Inherits | Terminal  | Running terminal commands in separate context     |
| Claude Code Guide | Haiku    | Read-only | Answering questions about Claude Code features    |

| Configuration            | Value                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Custom agent location    | `.claude/agents/*.md` (project), `~/.claude/agents/*.md` (user)                   |
| CLI agents               | `--agents '{...}'` (session only, JSON format)                                    |
| Plugin agents            | Plugin `agents/` directory (lowest priority)                                      |
| Required fields          | `name`, `description`                                                             |
| Optional fields          | `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `skills`, `hooks`, `color` |
| Model values             | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `inherit` (default)                                    |
| Permission modes         | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, `plan`                  |
| Nesting limit            | Subagents cannot spawn other subagents (one level only)                           |
| Foreground vs background | Foreground blocks main conversation; background runs concurrently                 |
| Batch size               | 5-8 items per agent (standard tasks)                                              |
| Parallel agents          | 2-4 simultaneously                                                                |

## When to Use Subagents vs Main Conversation

| Use Subagents When                                              | Use Main Conversation When                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Task produces verbose output (test suites, logs, API responses) | Task needs frequent back-and-forth or iterative refinement |
| Enforcing specific tool restrictions or permissions             | Multiple phases share significant context                  |
| Work is self-contained and can return a summary                 | Making a quick, targeted change                            |
| Parallel independent research paths                             | Latency matters (subagents start fresh and gather context) |

## Tool Access Patterns

| Agent Role         | Recommended Tools                       | Rationale                                     |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Read-only reviewer | `Read, Grep, Glob`                      | Cannot modify code; safe for audits           |
| File creator       | `Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep`         | NO Bash; avoids heredoc approval spam         |
| Script runner      | `Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash`   | Full access for build/deploy tasks            |
| Research agent     | `Read, Grep, Glob, WebFetch, WebSearch` | External data access for documentation lookup |

Subagents inherit all tools by default (including MCP tools). Use `tools` as an allowlist or `disallowedTools` as a denylist to restrict access. MCP tools are not available in background subagents.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                                     | Correct Pattern                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Expecting subagents to spawn sub-subagents                  | Subagents cannot nest; chain subagents from the main conversation instead                                  |
| Giving Bash tool to agents that only create files           | Use Write and Edit tools only; Bash causes approval spam from heredoc usage                                |
| Omitting `disallowedTools` for sensitive operations         | Use `disallowedTools` to explicitly deny dangerous tools even when inheriting                              |
| Spawning too many agents (5+) for a small task              | Start with 2-3 agents; coordination overhead outweighs benefit at higher counts                            |
| Burying critical instructions past line 300 of agent prompt | Put critical rules immediately after frontmatter; models deprioritize late instructions                    |
| Using specialized agents for large-scale software dev       | Use fungible agents with a shared task board; specialized agents create single points of failure           |
| Not including "FIX issues found" in delegation prompts      | Without explicit action directive, agents only report problems without making changes                      |
| Setting model to Haiku for content generation               | Default to Sonnet; Haiku only for script execution, fast lookups, or pass/fail checks                      |
| Not writing clear descriptions for custom agents            | Claude uses the `description` field to decide when to auto-delegate; vague descriptions prevent delegation |
| Using MCP tools in background subagents                     | MCP tools are not available in background subagents; run in foreground instead                             |
| Not preloading skills into subagents                        | Subagents do not inherit skills from the parent; list them explicitly in the `skills` field                |

## Delegation

- **Explore codebase before designing agent prompts**: Claude auto-delegates to the built-in Explore subagent (Haiku, read-only) for file discovery and code search; supports quick, medium, and very thorough modes
- **Plan multi-agent architecture for complex projects**: Use plan mode; Claude delegates research to the Plan subagent before presenting a plan
- **Execute batch operations across many files**: Chain General-purpose subagents from the main conversation with identical prompts and non-overlapping item lists
- **Isolate high-volume operations**: Delegate test runs, log processing, or doc fetching to subagents to keep verbose output out of your main context
- **Run parallel research**: Spawn multiple subagents simultaneously for independent investigations; Claude synthesizes findings when all complete
- **Resume interrupted work**: Ask Claude to continue a previous subagent; resumed agents retain full conversation history including tool calls and reasoning

Use when reviewing code for vulnerabilities, implementing auth patterns, securing APIs, configuring security headers, hardening supply chain, preventing injection attacks, or preparing for compliance audits.'

# Security

Security is built-in, not bolted-on. Every feature, endpoint, and data flow must consider security implications.

## OWASP Top 10 (2025)

| #   | Vulnerability                      | Prevention                                      |
| --- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Broken Access Control              | Verify permissions server-side, default deny    |
| 2   | Security Misconfiguration          | Secure defaults, remove unused features         |
| 3   | Software Supply Chain Failures     | SBOM, dependency scanning, signed builds        |
| 4   | Cryptographic Failures             | Use TLS, hash passwords (argon2id), encrypt PII |
| 5   | Injection                          | Parameterized queries, input validation         |
| 6   | Insecure Design                    | Threat modeling, security requirements          |
| 7   | Authentication Failures            | Strong passwords, MFA, secure session mgmt      |
| 8   | Software or Data Integrity         | Verify dependencies, sign releases              |
| 9   | Logging and Alerting Failures      | Log security events, set up alerts              |
| 10  | Mishandling Exceptional Conditions | Fail securely, generic errors to clients        |

## Security Principles

| Principle          | Rule                                                      |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Defense in Depth   | Multiple layers: firewall, auth, authz, encryption, audit |
| Least Privilege    | Minimum permissions needed, nothing more                  |
| Zero Trust         | Never trust, always verify. Assume breach.                |
| Secure by Default  | HTTPS, strict passwords, secure cookies out of the box    |
| Fail Securely      | Access denied on error, no internal details to users      |
| Validate on Server | Client validation is UX, server validation is security    |

## Pre-Deployment Checklist

| Area          | Requirements                                                        |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Passwords     | Hashed with argon2id (preferred) or bcrypt (12+ rounds)             |
| Tokens        | JWT with EdDSA/ES256, 15min access / 7d refresh, httpOnly cookies   |
| Sessions      | HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies                           |
| Rate Limiting | Auth endpoints: 5 attempts/15min                                    |
| Authorization | All routes check auth server-side, default deny                     |
| Input         | Validated with schema (Zod), parameterized SQL                      |
| Uploads       | Whitelist types, enforce size limits                                |
| Secrets       | No secrets in code or VCS                                           |
| Headers       | CSP (with nonces), HSTS, Permissions-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options |
| CORS          | Configured restrictively                                            |
| Encryption    | PII encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3)            |
| Logging       | Audit logging for security events                                   |
| Dependencies  | SBOM generated, `npm audit` clean, Dependabot enabled               |

## Threat Modeling (STRIDE)

| Threat                 | Category        | Key Mitigations                                        |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Spoofing               | Authentication  | MFA, strong passwords, JWT with short expiry           |
| Tampering              | Integrity       | Input validation, HTTPS/TLS, signed tokens             |
| Repudiation            | Accountability  | Audit logging, digital signatures                      |
| Info Disclosure        | Confidentiality | Encryption, least privilege, secret management         |
| Denial of Service      | Availability    | Rate limiting, input validation, CDN/DDoS protection   |
| Elevation of Privilege | Authorization   | Authz checks on every request, ABAC, permission audits |

## Risk Levels

| Level    | Action                    |
| -------- | ------------------------- |
| Critical | Immediate action required |
| High     | Address before launch     |
| Medium   | Address post-launch       |
| Low      | Monitor, may accept risk  |

## Compliance Overview

| Framework | Scope              | Key Requirements                                                   |
| --------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| GDPR      | EU data subjects   | Consent, data subject rights, breach notification (72h), DPIA      |
| HIPAA     | US healthcare data | PHI encryption, RBAC, audit logs, BAA with providers               |
| SOC 2     | SaaS customer data | Security policies, MFA, encryption, incident response              |
| PCI-DSS   | Credit card data   | Use payment processor (Stripe), tokenization, network segmentation |

## Anti-Patterns

| Anti-Pattern                                  | Fix                                              |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Security as afterthought                      | Integrate from design phase                      |
| Client-side authorization                     | Always verify permissions server-side            |
| Trusting client data (e.g., userId from body) | Get user ID from authenticated session           |
| Rolling your own crypto                       | Use proven libraries (argon2, bcrypt, libsodium) |
| Compliance = security                         | Compliance is the minimum; security is ongoing   |
| Verbose error responses                       | Generic messages to clients, details server-side |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                                       | Correct Pattern                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Performing authorization checks only on the client side       | Always verify permissions server-side; client checks are UX only    |
| Trusting user-supplied IDs from request body (e.g., userId)   | Derive user identity from the authenticated session or token        |
| Rolling custom cryptography instead of using proven libraries | Use argon2id, bcrypt, or libsodium for all cryptographic operations |
| Treating compliance certification as equivalent to security   | Compliance is the minimum bar; security requires ongoing review     |
| Returning verbose error messages with stack traces to clients | Show generic messages to clients; log details server-side only      |

## Delegation

- **Scan codebase for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities and insecure patterns**: Use `Explore` agent to search for SQL injection, XSS, and hardcoded secrets
- **Implement authentication, authorization, and security headers end-to-end**: Use `Task` agent to configure JWT, RBAC, CSP, HSTS, and rate limiting
- **Design a threat model and security architecture for new features**: Use `Plan` agent to apply STRIDE methodology and map trust boundaries

> For database-layer security (RLS policies, Postgres/Supabase hardening, audit trails), use the `database-security` skill. For AI/LLM security (prompt injection defense, agentic zero-trust, MCP tool hardening), use the `secure-ai` skill.

- [Threat Modeling](references/threat-modeling.md) — STRIDE methodology, risk assessment process, trust boundaries
- [Authentication and Authorization](references/auth.md) — JWT, session-based, OAuth, RBAC, ABAC, IDOR protection
- [API Security](references/api-security.md) — OWASP API Security Top 10, object-level authorization, rate limiting, SSRF prevention, security testing
- [Input Validation](references/input-validation.md) — SQL injection, XSS, command injection, path traversal, Zod validation, file upload security
- [Data Protection](references/data-protection.md) — Password hashing (argon2id/bcrypt), AES-256-GCM encryption, secrets management
- [Secure Configuration](references/secure-config.md) — Security headers, CORS, Express hardening, rate limiting
- [Supply Chain Security](references/supply-chain.md) — SBOM generation, dependency scanning, CI/CD hardening, artifact signing
- [Monitoring and Compliance](references/monitoring-compliance.md) — Audit logging, error handling, GDPR/HIPAA/SOC2/PCI-DSS, troubleshooting

Includes axum web framework, ratatui terminal UI, clap CLI parsing, criterion benchmarking, cargo-deny supply chain security, cargo-dist binary distribution, and release-plz changelog automation.

  Use when writing Rust code, designing ownership models, building async services with Tokio/axum, creating terminal UIs with ratatui, setting up CLI applications with clap, configuring CI/CD pipelines for Rust, benchmarking with criterion, auditing dependencies with cargo-deny, or distributing binaries with cargo-dist.

# Rust

## Overview

Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.

**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
| Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
| `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
| Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

## Delegation

- **Code exploration**: Use `Explore` agent
- **Architecture review**: Use `Task` agent
- **Code review**: Delegate to `code-reviewer` agent

> If the `docker` skill is available, delegate multi-stage container build patterns to it.
> If the `github-actions` skill is available, delegate CI pipeline configuration to it.
> If the `openapi` skill is available, delegate API specification and code generation to it.

- [Ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, and type system patterns](references/ownership-and-types.md)
- [Error handling with Result, Option, thiserror, and anyhow](references/error-handling.md)
- [Async programming with Tokio runtime and concurrency](references/async-tokio.md)
- [Web APIs and backends with axum, tower, and sqlx](references/axum-web.md)
- [Terminal user interfaces with ratatui and crossterm](references/ratatui-tui.md)
- [CLI applications with clap, config, and signal handling](references/cli-applications.md)
- [Testing patterns and criterion benchmarking](references/testing-and-benchmarks.md)
- [Release pipeline with cargo-deny, cargo-dist, and release-plz](references/release-pipeline.md)

# Rust

## Overview

Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.

**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
| Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
| `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
| Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

## Delegation

- **Code exploration**: Use `Explore` agent
- **Architecture review**: Use `Task` agent
- **Code review**: Delegate to `code-reviewer` agent

> If the `docker` skill is available, delegate multi-stage container build patterns to it.
> If the `github-actions` skill is available, delegate CI pipeline configuration to it.
> If the `openapi` skill is available, delegate API specification and code generation to it.

- [Async programming with Tokio runtime and concurrency](references/async-tokio.md)
- [Web APIs and backends with axum, tower, and sqlx](references/axum-web.md)
- [Terminal user interfaces with ratatui and crossterm](references/ratatui-tui.md)
- [CLI applications with clap, config, and signal handling](references/cli-applications.md)
- [Testing patterns and criterion benchmarking](references/testing-and-benchmarks.md)
- [Release pipeline with cargo-deny, cargo-dist, and release-plz](references/release-pipeline.md)

6. **Interrupted stages fail closed, but do not constitute complete resume support.** Important intents are preserved, yet the shell interfaces mostly require manual reconciliation rather than implementing phase-aware recovery.

These findings establish integration defects and requirement conflicts. They do **not** establish which defect was the last encountered runtime failure, nor prove that no supported no-loop implementation exists.

## Architecture and stage ownership

The existing chatbot path is:

```text
existing caller-bound 3tchedFS
  → identity_sled.prepare_container
  → local native-preparation receipt
  → prepare-instance-disk: create / prepare
  → sync-instance-upgrade: pair
  → bind-instance-root
  → prepare-chatbot-adoption
  → identity_sled.provision_container [separate operation]
  → authoritative identity/native/storage adoption [Rust owner]
  → authorized start [separate lifecycle operation]

base identity-roots service
  → select completed boot receipt
  → restore-chatbot-root
  → sync-instance-upgrade boot
  → stopped root restored and synchronized
```

A second, older branch remains in `op-identity-root`:

```text
seed-create → seed-up/check → seed-lungs → explicit boot attestation
```

It uses a writable Btrfs sprout root and host-created FUSE mount, rather than the newer read-only upgrade-over-seed overlay and guest-owned FUSE mounts. These are **different contracts**, not interchangeable recovery routes.

## Additional integration defects and retained semantics

### 1. The two-FUSE-view image cannot satisfy the binder’s one-entry validator

Image input, `S/deploy/workspace-image/3tchedfs.fstab:2-3`:

```fstab
3tchedFS /run/mount/3tchedfs fuse.3tchedFS noauto,rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime 0 0
threetched /run/mount/threetched fuse.3tchedFS noauto,rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime 0 0
```

Binder, `S/deploy/scripts/bind-instance-root.sh:171-183`:

```awk
            if ($1=="3tchedFS" || $2=="/run/mount/3tchedfs" || $3=="fuse.3tchedFS") {
                count++
                if ($1!="3tchedFS" || $2!="/run/mount/3tchedfs" || $3!="fuse.3tchedFS" ||
                    $5!="0" || $6!="0" || (NF>6 && $7 !~ /^#/)) bad=1
```

```awk
        END { if (bad || count!=1) exit 1 }
```

The second entry matches by filesystem type, increments the count and fails the source/mountpoint test. The `seen` options map also spans entries, so simply changing `count!=1` to `count!=2` is insufficient.

**Concrete change:** update this existing validator to recognize exactly the two supported source/target tuples, validate each tuple exactly once, reset per-entry option tracking, retain the exact six options, and continue rejecting active host-storage entries and unknown FUSE tuples. Apply the same effective-fstab check during stopped synchronization/restoration.

The installed binder has the same one-entry contract.

### 2. Agent links point to the explicitly excluded view

`S/deploy/workspace-image/prepare-lungs-client.sh:66-70`:

```sh
upstream_plugins=threetched,tched_router
"$client" --store "$store" capture --schema-only --catalog "$catalog" --state "$empty" \
    --exclude-plugin "$upstream_plugins"
"$client" --store "$upstream_store" capture --schema-only --catalog "$catalog" --state "$empty" \
    --include-plugin "$upstream_plugins"
```

But `S/deploy/workspace-agent/populate.sh:48-50` creates:

```sh
ln -s /run/mount/3tchedfs/plugins/threetched "$base/@agent_shared/threetched-plugins"
ln -s /run/mount/3tchedfs/plugins/tched_router "$base/@agent_skills/runtime"
ln -s /run/mount/3tchedfs/plugins/threetched "$base/@agent_skills/skills"
```

**Concrete change:** those three upstream-plugin links belong under `/run/mount/threetched/plugins/...`; cognitive and `agent_config` links remain under `/run/mount/3tchedfs`. Update the existing image/workspace documentation accordingly. Do not edit an accepted immutable seed in place to apply this correction.

### 3. Old sprout helper is not a compatible fallback for the canonical guest-FUSE container

The current binder requires the canonical local/expanded device:

```jq
.fuse=={type:"unix-char",source:"/dev/fuse",path:"/dev/fuse"}
```

`S/deploy/scripts/bind-instance-root.sh:120-124`.

The old/current shared-sprout helper instead requires:

```jq
(.expanded_devices | type == "object" and length > 0 and all(.[]; .type == "disk"))
```

`S/deploy/runit/libexec-3tched/op-identity-root:755`.

Its profile/device-key whitelist excludes `fuse`, and `seed-lungs` creates a **host FUSE mount** with `--lungs-session`, then exposes it as an Incus disk at **`/run/mount/3tchedFS`**. See `:700-726,967-1025`.

That differs from the image’s two guest-owned mounts and `BindCurrentContainer` behavior.

**Concrete change:** keep legacy receipt interpretation observational where necessary, but do not route a failed canonical candidate into `seed-lungs` or loosen the device allowlist indiscriminately. The selected existing workflow must use one agreed guest-FUSE/native-device contract.

### 4. Seed permanence and no-host-loops conflict with actual helper behavior

The actual one-time membership operation is:

`S/deploy/runit/libexec-3tched/op-identity-root:1241`.

### 5. Correct root composition must not be simplified away

The newer root is:

```sh
mount -t overlay overlay -o "ro,lowerdir=$upgrade_layer:$seed_layer" "$view"
```

`S/deploy/scripts/bind-instance-root.sh:262`.

There is **no overlay upper/work directory**. The persistent writable leaf is the writable member of the sprout filesystem. Private agent subvolumes and `@agent_user/persist` are separately bound; shared/soul are read-only.

`sync-instance-upgrade.sh:329-407` retains immutable received snapshots, publishes a writable clone as replica `@`, verifies clone ancestry, exposes both OS lowers read-only and restores sibling/persistence mounts.

Preserve these distinctions:

- writable sprout member ≠ OverlayFS upper;
- writable replica filesystem/clone ≠ writable guest OS root;
- received snapshot ≠ published clone;
- immutable shared seed ≠ per-instance root copy.

The sync helper notes that deleting seed files requires whiteouts in the upgrade layer. It transports snapshots; it does **not** generate deletion whiteouts. Source excerpts alone therefore do not establish that the prepared upgrade stream encodes all required deletion semantics.

The binder checks the replica mount is Btrfs FSROOT `/`, but does not compare its live FSID to `.upgrade_fsid` before binding it (`bind-instance-root.sh:77-84`). Its final root check verifies overlay type, not the full source identity, lower order, modes and sibling binds (`:275-280`).

The following uses an **illustrative volume name and guest path**, not an observed existing volume:

```yaml
devices:
  upgrade-replica:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    source: identity-upgrade
    path: /upgrade
    readonly: "true"
    required: "true"
```

Conditions:

- `identity-upgrade` must exist as an Incus **custom volume with `filesystem` content**.
- Pool backing must satisfy no-host-loops.
- Ownership/idmapping must be compatible with the existing unprivileged container.
- Send/receive, publication, ancestry, recovery, and pairing proofs remain separate obligations.

**This merely exposes a filesystem at `/upgrade`. It does not place that filesystem above the seed in `/`.** Its `readonly` mount option also does not by itself make a Btrfs snapshot suitable as an incremental-send baseline.

The version-matched documentation states:

> “Custom storage volumes of … content type … `block` or `iso` cannot be attached to containers, but only to virtual machines.”

Source: [Incus 7.0.1 storage volumes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lxc/incus/v7.0.1/doc/howto/storage_volumes.md).

Thus the presence of a `custom_block_volumes` API extension in a receipt is **not** proof that a custom block volume can be attached to this container.

### D. Arbitrary host root `source`: explicitly unsupported

Do **not** present this as valid:

```yaml
devices:
  root:
    type: disk
    source: /some/prepared/root-view
    path: /
```

Incus 7.0.1 validation contains the exact errors:

> `Root disk entry may not have a "source" property set`

> `Root disk entry must have a "pool" property set`

Source: [disk.go:513–519](https://github.com/lxc/incus/blob/v7.0.1/internal/server/device/disk.go#L513-L519).

Likewise, a custom-volume `source` cannot simply be assigned to `path: /`.

### Pool backing without a loop is supported independently

Version-matched Incus configuration documents pool `source` as:

> “Path to an existing block device, loop file or Btrfs subvolume”

Source: [Incus 7.0.1 config_options.txt:5761–5767](https://github.com/lxc/incus/blob/v7.0.1/doc/config_options.txt#L5761-L5767).

Therefore an authorized existing Btrfs subvolume on non-loop storage can support the **pool layer** without introducing new LVM or a VM. Merely changing a source string does not migrate the existing pool, and this capability does not solve the sprout writable-member requirement.

---

## 4. Why the seed contract needs block storage

Upstream describes a seeding device as:

> “extending a read-only filesystem on a device with another device that captures all writes.”

It further states:

> “Mounting such device will not allow any writes, except adding a new device by **btrfs device add**.”

Source: [Btrfs seeding-device documentation](https://btrfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Seeding-device.html).

The device documentation identifies Btrfs storage as one or more **block devices**. The subvolume documentation distinguishes subvolumes from block-level logical volumes:

> “A subvolume in BTRFS is not like an LVM logical volume, which is block-level snapshot while BTRFS subvolumes are file extent-based.”

Sources: [btrfs-device](https://btrfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/btrfs-device.html), [btrfs-subvolume](https://btrfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/btrfs-subvolume.html).

## Invariants

Sources: recovery/BackendProof.md architecture and §§3–4; recovery/SourceChain.md failure/resume and base boot sections. These are saved source investigations, not fresh runtime receipts.

## Coordinated edits, not a shell-only workaround

1. **provision-workspace-subscriber.sh:** make post-bootstrap progression and completion boundaries explicit. Reconcile the existing native operation and UUID. Carry one verified storage descriptor through preparation, pairing, binding, adoption and requested start. Native preparation alone must never be labelled provisioned.

4. **bind-instance-root.sh:** validate both guest FUSE views, live replica FSID, exact lower order/modes/idmap and all effective sibling/persistence bindings. Reconcile retained intent; do not rerun mounts blindly.
5. **prepare-chatbot-adoption.sh and identity_clean_provision.rs:** change the plan representation together. An image-free layout cannot claim file inode/GPT/loop evidence. Distinguish its version/type explicitly; retain deny_unknown_fields, digest, revision predecessor, native UUID/ETag, seed FSID/generation, inherited members, persistence and upgrade ancestry. Do not replay fresh-genesis behavior against existing identity state.
6. **identity_clean_provision/storage.rs and partitioned.rs:** replace loop-specific proofs with equally strong held-descriptor proofs for the selected primitive. Verify actual protected seed and writable-member identities, access modes and complete ancestry; reject loop-backed ancestry. Keep seed SEEDING/generation/block-RO, exact member closure, ordinary persistence directory and native bind equality. If physical partitions remain, prove genuine parent/geometry; if separate objects replace partitions, prove their distinct ownership rather than fabricating GPT fields. Do not delete security checks simply to accept subvolumes.
7. **Cozo identity_transactions/clean_provision.rs:** recognize only the new proven layout; retain deterministic digest operation, exact predecessor CAS, replay equivalence, publication recovery and completed-binding immutability. No grant broadening or direct Cozo patch.
8. **restore-chatbot-root and identity-roots/run:** use one selected helper closure/storage contract; preflight all selections. Link boot authorization to adopted UUID, revision, storage proof and explicit power policy. Running instances are observation-only; stopped restoration must not allocate members. Base-service installation is separate from application staging. Never add an application ownership marker just to force the base service into golden.
9. **prepare-lungs-client.sh, binder fstab validator, populate.sh and image metadata/docs:** align both guest views, schema-only stores and socket binding without capturing credentials. Explicitly distinguish older and newer layout metadata and align release-ID producer/consumer validation. Configured service files are not mounted identity-bound operations.
10. **attach-host-workspace-folders, if retained in this workflow:** accept the exact permitted FUSE device alongside allowed disks; its disk-only observation conflicts with canonical native configuration. It is not a prerequisite for native creation.

## Native declaration to preserve

This is an excerpt of the existing historical native contract, not a complete replacement YAML and not proof of present installed equality. Source: original Hermes record 3077, exported physical line 80 of `20261018_222032_11fb9b.jsonl`, historical incus.rs:1464–1493; corroborating native_container_creation.rs:106–124 (BackendProof §1).

```yaml
type: container
ephemeral: false
source:
  type: none
profiles:
  - 3tched-lungs
config:
  security.privileged: "false"
  security.nesting: "false"
  security.protection.shift: "true"
  boot.autostart: "false"
  security.syscalls.deny_default: "true"
devices:
  root:
    type: disk
    pool: identity-roots
    path: /
  runtime-run:
    type: disk
    source: "tmpfs:"
    path: /run
  fuse:
    type: unix-char
    source: /dev/fuse
    path: /dev/fuse
```

Retain existing identity metadata, raw.lxc UTS binding, idmap and all three storage-ioctl denials; their absence from this excerpt is not a removal. Profile config remains empty; profile devices include runtime-run with initial.mode 0755 and readonly lungs-socket-dir from/to `/run/opdbus/lungs`. Never flatten expanded configuration into a blind replacement. Existing root pool is verified as `dir` at `/var/lib/incus-storage/identity-roots`; changing it to a Btrfs pool is a storage migration, not a one-line repair.

## Unresolved topology — smallest decision

Start from the owner's demonstrated mechanism: **the seed supplies backing; `btrfs device add <writable-device> <mounted-seed-path>` adds the writable member, followed by the sprout's read-write mount.** Historical `op-identity-root:1172–1196` confirms the sequence and preservation of inherited sibling identities. Trace the writable member/Cozo association separately from the Incus subvolume presentation and upgrade replica. Do not reject the complete subvolume arrangement merely because a subvolume is not itself the device-add operand. Preserve no-host-loops while identifying the actual required backing and proofs; historical loop variables are not authorization to restore loops. Investigate the documented seed-mount constraint against that concrete topolog…

All-host no-loop also requires a separately authorized, data-preserving resolution of existing pool backing. No detachment or migration is authorized here. Preserve the seed; do not silently retire it, copy it, clear its flag or replace it with snapshots.

## Acceptance evidence for future authorized implementation

Independent receipts must distinguish source, built artifact, installed application helpers, installed base service, operation acceptance, authoritative adoption, actual startup and cold restoration. Verify no loops across the complete backing chain, immutable seed/member provenance, isolated persistence, upgrade ancestry/lower ordering, admission denial behavior, uncertain-outcome reconciliation and power policy. These are future acceptance requirements, not tests or runtime operations executed in this diagnostic run.

1003:seed_attach() {

1010:        seed_verify_loop "$seed_view" "$seed_device" 1
